splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year or whether actuaries may select assumptions after that date. The outcome affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be selected by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that a plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date, allowing use of more current data.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the period of court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year and raises questions about the limits of judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when the supervisee absconds, so the supervised release period does not run during the time the person is a fugitive.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is not tolled during absconding because there is no statutory authority for such tolling, and the term expires as stated in the judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: A longstanding 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether federal prisoners face an additional gatekeeping requirement under § 2244(b)(1) when bringing successive collateral attacks on their convictions. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners are categorically barred from raising any previously presented claim, on top of § 2255(h)'s separate requirements. If it does not apply, prisoners need only satisfy § 2255(h).

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the § 2244(b)(1) bar on relitigating previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, categorically barring any claim that was previously presented.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, so they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits have disagreed on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. Some circuits have recognized candidate standing based on competitive injury, while others have required a more concrete showing of harm. The resolution affects whether election-rule challenges can be brought before an election or must wait until afterwards.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates suffer a cognizable competitive injury sufficient for Article III standing when a state changes election rules in ways that may affect the outcome of the race.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Jacobson v. Florida Secretary of State

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates must show more than a generalized competitive injury to establish standing, and that speculative claims about how ballot-counting rules might affect an election outcome are insufficient.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations of ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's commentary interpreting ambiguous Guidelines provisions (under Kisor/Stinson deference) or instead apply the rule of lenity in favor of the defendant. At least three circuits hold that lenity trumps deference, while others (including the Third Circuit) have held that deference trumps lenity. The issue has grown more significant after Loper Bright overruled Chevron.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity should resolve ambiguity in criminal sentencing provisions before courts defer to agency or Commission interpretations, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability through delegated power.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's authoritative commentary interpreting ambiguous Guidelines, even if such deference results in a broader reading unfavorable to the defendant.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to be met for disqualification) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: A deep circuit split exists on whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), or whether possessing any one of the criteria is disqualifying. This affects mandatory minimum sentencing for drug offenses and leads to disparate sentencing outcomes depending on where a defendant is prosecuted.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria, reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as 'or' in context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which includes inchoate offenses like conspiracy in the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is entitled to deference when the guideline text does not mention inchoate offenses.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary expanding 'controlled substance offense' to include conspiracy and other inchoate offenses deserves controlling weight under Stinson/Kisor deference, or whether the guideline text unambiguously excludes such offenses. This affects career-offender enhancements and substantially impacts sentencing ranges.

positions.label: Commentary is entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1's inclusion of inchoate offenses is a reasonable interpretation of genuinely ambiguous guideline text and is entitled to controlling weight under Stinson and Kisor.

positions.label: Commentary exceeds guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and that Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the definition beyond the text, so it is not entitled to deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state statute criminalizes a substance not listed on the federal Controlled Substances Act schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires that the substance underlying a state conviction also be controlled under federal law. Some circuits read the Guidelines broadly to include any state drug offense, while others require a federal-state match. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements.

positions.label: State offense qualifies regardless of federal schedules
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines broadly define 'controlled substance offense' to include 'an offense under state law,' with no textual basis to graft a federal-law limitation onto the guideline.

positions.label: Substance must also be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction does not qualify as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines if the substance at issue is not also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may impose a sentence upon revocation of supervised release that expressly punishes the defendant for the violation, or whether revocation sentences must be limited to sanctioning the breach of trust.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit allows district courts to expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release, placing it at one extreme of a circuit split. Other circuits hold that revocation sentences should be focused on the breach of the court's trust inherent in the violation, not on punishing the underlying conduct. This affects hundreds of revocation proceedings annually.

positions.label: Punishment for the violation is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may impose revocation sentences that expressly punish defendants for their violations of supervised release conditions.

positions.label: Revocation should sanction breach of trust, not punish
positions.summary: Holds that the purpose of revocation sentencing is to sanction the defendant's breach of the court's trust, not to punish the defendant for the underlying violative conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for an order on a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees in a criminal case is governed by the civil appeal timeline (30 days) or the criminal appeal timeline (14 days).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (triggering a 30-day appeal deadline) or part of the criminal case itself (triggering a 14-day deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined what it described as the majority view holding the civil deadline applies.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies (30 days)
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies (14 days)
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is part of the criminal proceeding, so the shorter criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for a sentence reduction under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law can contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release. Some circuits categorically bar reliance on such changes, while others allow them, at least in combination with other factors. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment (§ 1B1.13(b)(6)) attempted to permit it, but some circuits hold the Commission exceeded its authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot constitute an extraordinary and compelling reason for a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A), and that the Sentencing Commission's contrary policy statement exceeds its statutory authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered, at least in combination with other factors, as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's assets belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon a good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether property appreciation that occurs between a Chapter 13 filing and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held that appreciation belongs to the estate based on § 541(a)'s broad definition of estate property, creating a split with other circuits that protect the debtor's interest in post-petition appreciation upon good-faith conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that under § 348(f)(1)(A), post-petition pre-conversion appreciation in asset value belongs to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion, based on § 541(a)'s broad scope.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that § 348(f)(1)(A) protects good-faith converting debtors by limiting the estate to the value of property as of the original petition date, so post-petition appreciation belongs to the debtor.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a federal prisoner's challenge to conditions of confinement — specifically BOP decisions regarding transfer to prerelease custody under the First Step Act — must be brought as a habeas corpus petition under 28 U.S.C. § 2241 or may be brought as a civil rights action.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether challenges to the terms and conditions of confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of imprisonment) are cognizable only in habeas or may also be pursued through civil rights actions. The issue has been applied to First Step Act earned time credits disputes, where some circuits require habeas and others permit Bivens or § 2241 claims interchangeably.

positions.label: Habeas is the proper vehicle
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to BOP decisions affecting the duration of custody, including application of First Step Act time credits for early transfer to prerelease custody, must be brought as habeas corpus petitions under § 2241.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: Woodall v. Federal Bureau of Prisons

positions.label: Civil rights action is also available
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to conditions of confinement, including BOP placement decisions, may be brought as civil rights actions and are not limited to habeas corpus.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that denials of motions to seal medical records qualify for immediate appeal under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of 'high order' that would be irreparably lost without immediate review. This creates a potential tension with other circuits that have applied the collateral order doctrine more narrowly to sealing orders.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal medical records are immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because maintaining medical privacy is a value of high order that cannot be vindicated after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders related to sealing documents are generally not immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because the privacy interest can be protected through other procedural mechanisms.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Apple Inc. v. Samsung Electronics Co.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a federal prisoner's claim seeking application of earned time credits under the First Step Act for expedited transfer to prerelease custody can be brought as a habeas corpus petition under 28 U.S.C. § 2241.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether federal prisoners may use habeas corpus to challenge BOP decisions regarding the application of First Step Act time credits. This implicates the broader, longstanding circuit split on the boundary between habeas and civil rights remedies for prisoners challenging terms of confinement that affect release timing.

positions.label: Habeas under § 2241 is available
positions.summary: Holds that claims seeking expedited transfer to prerelease custody based on FSA time credits challenge the duration of confinement and are properly brought as habeas corpus petitions under § 2241.

positions.label: Habeas under § 2241 is not the proper vehicle
positions.summary: Holds that FSA time-credit claims concerning transfer to prerelease custody do not challenge the fact or duration of confinement and thus must be brought through other means, such as the APA or Bivens.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The Second Circuit's approach to legal standards for discrimination liability and damages in hospitality and business establishments was found sufficiently unsettled to warrant Supreme Court review. The decision could impact hospitality, retail, and service industries nationwide by establishing or refining standards for fair treatment and available remedies.

positions.label: Second Circuit approach
positions.summary: Applied a particular framework for evaluating discrimination claims in hospitality establishments that other circuits may not follow.

positions.label: Other circuits' approach
positions.summary: Other circuits apply different standards for evaluating discrimination claims and available remedies in public accommodation and hospitality contexts.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
